title: Men and Women Need Different Diets to Live Longer. A 104,000-Person Study Just Proved It.
excerpt: Coffee extends male lifespan by up to three years. Fish does the same for women. Both sexes benefit from cutting processed food — but the optimal longevity diet is not one-size-fits-all, and the South Asian kitchen may already hold the advantage.
body:
The dietary advice has always been frustratingly unisex. Eat your five a day. Cut the red meat. Choose whole grains. The assumption baked into decades of public health guidance is that what is good for one body is good for all bodies.

A sweeping new study from Queen Mary University of London, published in the journal Science Advances, has just dismantled that assumption with data from nearly 104,000 middle-aged adults tracked over more than a decade through the UK Biobank. The headline finding: the optimal diet for longevity is different for men and women, and getting the distinction right could add up to three years to your life.

## Coffee for Him, Fish for Her

The researchers analysed five established dietary patterns — including the Alternate Healthy Eating Index, the Mediterranean diet, the DASH diet, and the Diabetes Risk Reduction Diet (DRRD) — and measured their associations with mortality and life expectancy.

Both sexes benefited substantially from the basics: more fruits, vegetables, nuts, seeds, and beans; less red meat, processed meat, white bread, fried foods, and ready meals. The right diet cut the risk of premature death by up to 24 per cent overall.

But the optimal pattern diverged sharply by sex.

Men lived longest on the Diabetes Risk Reduction Diet, which prioritises cutting blood sugar through specific food choices — with a pronounced boost from coffee consumption. The antioxidants in coffee have been linked in multiple studies to protection of the brain, heart, and liver. For men following this pattern, the life expectancy gain at age 45 was up to three years compared to those with the poorest diets.

Women, meanwhile, fared best on the Alternate Mediterranean Diet, which emphasises higher protein intake through fish while minimising potato consumption. Fish delivers protein, omega-3 fatty acids, vitamins, and minerals in a low-calorie package. Potatoes, by contrast, are carbohydrate-dense and convert rapidly to sugar in the gut. For women, the gain was up to 2.3 years.

"Our findings underscore the advantages of healthy diets in prolonging life expectancy," wrote lead author Dr Jing Song. But the subtext is equally important: a diet tuned to biological sex performs measurably better than one that ignores it.

## What the South Asian Kitchen Already Knows

The study's findings will resonate with diaspora families in a way that generic Western dietary advice rarely does, because the traditional Indian kitchen already embodies many of the principles the researchers identified — often without the Mediterranean branding.

Consider the parallels. The DRRD that extended male lifespan emphasises blood sugar management. Indian diets built around dal, vegetables, bitter gourd, fenugreek, and turmeric — all well-documented for their glycaemic effects — already target this pathway. The daily coffee ritual in South Indian households, from filter kaapi to instant Bru, delivers the antioxidant punch the study credits with protecting male health.

For women, the Mediterranean diet's emphasis on fish and protein maps directly onto the coastal cuisines of Kerala, Goa, Bengal, and Mangalore, where fish is not a weekly indulgence but a daily staple. The study's suggestion to cut potatoes aligns with what Ayurvedic dietary traditions have long cautioned about starchy root vegetables in excess.

None of this means that South Asian diets are perfect. The study's universal advice — cut processed food, refined carbohydrates, and fried items — challenges the diaspora's growing reliance on convenience foods, packaged snacks, and restaurant meals. First-generation immigrants who maintained traditional cooking patterns may be inadvertently following a near-optimal longevity diet. Their children, raised on a hybrid of home cooking and Western processed food, may not be.

## The Genetic Wildcard

One of the study's most striking findings is that healthy dietary patterns extended life expectancy regardless of genetic predisposition to longevity. Participants with favourable longevity genes who also ate well gained the most years, but even those without genetic advantages saw significant gains from diet alone.

For South Asians, who carry elevated genetic risk for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome, this finding is particularly relevant. It suggests that dietary intervention can meaningfully offset genetic vulnerability — a message that cuts against the fatalism that sometimes accompanies discussions of "the South Asian gene."

The researchers studied 103,649 participants over a median follow-up of 10.6 years, during which 4,314 deaths were recorded. The five dietary patterns examined were scored and compared across quintiles, with life expectancy calculated at age 45.

## The Practical Takeaway

The study does not prescribe a single meal plan. What it offers is a framework: men should prioritise blood sugar management and lean into coffee; women should prioritise fish-based protein and reduce starchy carbohydrates. Both should build meals around plants, whole grains, nuts, and legumes while cutting processed and fried foods.

For diaspora families, the most actionable advice may be the simplest: cook more like your grandparents did, but with intentional adjustments for sex-specific needs. The longevity diet is not in a supplement bottle or a meal-kit subscription. It is, in many cases, already in the family recipe book.
